label: o8y7t626rf53deg23489jru3sgbref6
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $B = B_{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}};a_1,\dots,a_n}$.
For each $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$, $x_i \neq 0$ is homogeneous of degree $d_i$;
so $e(B) = \gcd(d_1,\dots,d_n) = \gcd( \frac{L}{a_1}, \dots, \frac{L}{a_n} ) = \frac{L}{ 	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}(a_1,\dots,a_n) } = 1$.
Define 
$$
\hat d_i = \gcd\big\{\, d_j \, \mid \, j \in J_i \, \big\} \quad \text{for each $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$.}
$$
Then $\hat d_1 = \gcd(d_2,\dots,d_n) \linebreak[3]= \gcd( \frac{L}{a_2}, \dots, \frac{L}{a_n} ) = \frac{L}{ 	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}(a_2,\dots,a_n) } = \frac{L}{L_1}$,
and by the same argument we get
$$
\textstyle
\hat d_i = \frac{L}{L_i} \quad \text{for all $i \in \{1,\dots n\}$.}
$$
If $i \neq j$ then $\gcd( L/L_i , L/L_j ) = \gcd(\hat d_i , \hat d_j ) = \gcd(d_1,\dots,d_n) = 1$, which proves (a).

(b)  We already proved that $e(B) = 1$.
If $Z$ denotes the set of height $1$ homogeneous prime ideals of $B$ then:
\begin{itemize}

\item for each $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$, some ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Z$ satisfies $x_i \in {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$;
\item for each ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Z$, at most one $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ satisfies $x_i \in {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$, 
and if  $x_i \in {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ then $e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) = \gcd\big\{\,d_j\, \mid \,j \in J_i\, \big\} = \hat d_i = L/L_i$.

\end{itemize}
It follows that $\big\{\, e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} ) \, \mid \, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Z \, \big\} = \{ 1,  \frac{L}{L_1}, \dots, \frac{L}{L_n} \}$,
so $\bar e(B) = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}\big( {\textstyle \frac{L}{L_1}, \dots, \frac{L}{L_n} } \big) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{L}{L_i}$, the last equality by (a). 
This proves (b), and (c) follows from (b).


(d)  Let $d$ be a divisor of $\bar e(B) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{L}{L_i}$.
Define $\alpha_i = \gcd(d,\hat d_i)$ for each $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$.
Let us prove that
\begin{equation}  \label {B09876543wexcvbjk0oijhnmlpAoiuy654321qws}
\text{for every $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$,} \qquad \gcd(d_i,\alpha_i)=1, \quad d \mid d_i \alpha_i  \quad \text{and} \quad  a_i = a_i' \alpha_i.
\end{equation}
Indeed, let $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$.
Since  $\alpha_i \mid \hat d_i$ and $\gcd(d_i,\hat d_i) = \gcd(d_1,\dots,d_n) = 1$, the first part of \eqref{B09876543wexcvbjk0oijhnmlpAoiuy654321qws} is clear.
To prove the second part, we first show that
\begin{equation}  \label {uhiw37ug3674g8239re0idk}
\textstyle \text{for all $j \in \{1,\dots,n\}$,\ \ $\frac{L}{L_j}$ divides $d_i \hat d_i$.}
\end{equation}
To see this, we note that $\frac{ d_i \hat d_i }{(L/L_j)} = \frac{ (L/a_i) (L/L_i) }{(L/L_j)} =  \frac{ L_j L }{a_i L_i} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$
because if $i=j$ then $a_i \mid L$ and $L_i \mid L_j$,
and if $i \neq j$ then $a_i \mid L_j$ and $L_i \mid L$. This proves \eqref{uhiw37ug3674g8239re0idk}.
By (a), (b) and \eqref{uhiw37ug3674g8239re0idk}, it follows that $\bar e(B) = \prod_{j=1}^n \frac{L}{L_j}$ divides $d_i \hat d_i$.
Since $d \mid \bar e(B)$, we obtain $d \mid d_i \hat d_i$, so $d$ divides $\gcd(d_i d, d_i \hat d_i) = d_i \gcd(d,\hat d_i) = d_i \alpha_i$,
which proves the second part of \eqref{B09876543wexcvbjk0oijhnmlpAoiuy654321qws}.
For the third part, note that $a_i' \alpha_i = \gcd( a_i, L_i ) \,  {\textstyle \left[ \frac{L/L_i}{ \gcd( d, L/L_i) } \right] } \, \gcd(d, \hat d_i )$
and $\hat d_i = \frac{L}{L_i}$, so $a_i' \alpha_i = \gcd( a_i, L_i ) (L/L_i)$.
On the other hand, 
$\frac{ a_i L_i }{ \gcd(a_i,L_i) } = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}(a_i,L_i) = L$, so $a_i = \gcd( a_i, L_i ) (L/L_i) = a_i'\alpha_i$,
proving \eqref{B09876543wexcvbjk0oijhnmlpAoiuy654321qws}.


Consider a monomial $m = x_1^{\nu_1} \cdots x_n^{\nu_n}$ ($\nu_1,\dots,\nu_n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$) such that $d$ divides $\deg(m)= d_1 \nu_1 + \cdots + d_n \nu_n$.
If $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ then  $\alpha_i \mid d_i \nu_i$ (because $\alpha_i \mid d \mid \deg(m)$ and $\alpha_i \mid \hat d_i$),
so $\alpha_i \mid \nu_i$ by \eqref{B09876543wexcvbjk0oijhnmlpAoiuy654321qws}. This shows that $m \in  {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}[x_1^{ \alpha_1 }, \dots, x_n^{ \alpha_n } ]$
and hence that $B^{(d)} \subseteq {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}[x_1^{ \alpha_1 }, \dots, x_n^{ \alpha_n } ]$.
By \eqref{B09876543wexcvbjk0oijhnmlpAoiuy654321qws}, we have $d \mid d_i \alpha_i$ and hence $x_i^{\alpha_i} \in B^{(d)}$ for all $i$,
so $B^{(d)} = {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}[x_1^{ \alpha_1 }, \dots, x_n^{ \alpha_n } ]$.
Observing that $( x_1^{ \alpha_1 } )^{a_1'} + \cdots + (x_n^{ \alpha_n })^{a_n'} = 0$ (again by \eqref{B09876543wexcvbjk0oijhnmlpAoiuy654321qws}),
one easily obtains that ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}[x_1^{ \alpha_1 }, \dots, x_n^{ \alpha_n } ] \overset{\text{\tiny$*$}}{\cong} B_{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}; a_1', \dots, a_n'}$.
This proves (d).

body_md:
Let $B = B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}; a_1, \dots, a_n}$.
Since (i) or (ii) holds and (i) implies (ii), (ii) holds. 
Cor.\ \ref{p98qy386e523brxhbfc6ghvc63x2345618q30} implies that $M(B) \subseteq D$,
and Lemma \ref{o8y7t626rf53deg23489jru3sgbref6}(d) implies that if $d \in D$ then
$B^{(d)} \overset{\text{\tiny$*$}}{\cong} B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}; f(d)}$ and consequently $B^{(d)}$ and $B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}; f(d)}$ have the same rigidity status.
By (ii) and \eqref{7y2ew6t2ewoqpoqbgfccxv27}, $B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}; f(d)}$ is rigid if and only if $f(d) \in \Gamma_n$, so:
\begin{equation}  \label {9876543erfcnbvc9x87654}
\text{for each $d \in D$, \quad $d \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$ if and only if  $f(d) \notin \Gamma_n$.}
\end{equation}
Since  $f(1)=(a_1,\dots,a_n) \in \Gamma_n$, \eqref{9876543erfcnbvc9x87654} implies that $1 \notin 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$, so $1 \notin M(B)$.

Also note that $L = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}(a_i,L_i) = a_i L_i / \gcd(a_i,L_i)$ for each $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$, so
\begin{equation}  \label {7236yhwebdcv5172wu}
L/L_i = a_i / \gcd(a_i,L_i) \quad \text{for all $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$.}
\end{equation}
Define the sets
$$
U_1 = \big\{\, a_i \, \mid \, i \in I_1 \, \big\} \quad \text{and} \quad  U_2 = \big\{\, \textstyle \frac{a_ia_j}4 \, \mid \, i,j \in I_2 \text{ and } i \neq j\, \big\} .
$$

Suppose that $i \in I_1$. Then \eqref{7236yhwebdcv5172wu} gives $L/L_i = a_i$,
so $a_i \in D$ and the tuple $f(a_i) = (a_1', \dots, a_n')$ satisfies $a_i'=1$ by \eqref{6gvhb3ag2n60b6tm9rn83h76b54};
so $f(a_i) \notin \Gamma_n$ and hence $a_i \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$ by \eqref{9876543erfcnbvc9x87654}. Thus,
\begin{equation}  \label {987432sdxcpo09287h6hxcve}
U_1 \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B) .
\end{equation}



Suppose that $1,2 \in I_2$.
For each $i \in \{1,2\}$ we have $\frac{a_i}2 = \frac L{L_i}$ by \eqref{7236yhwebdcv5172wu}, so $\frac{a_1 a_2}{4} = \frac L{L_1}  \frac L{L_2} \in D$
and, by \eqref{6gvhb3ag2n60b6tm9rn83h76b54}, the tuple $f(\frac{a_1 a_2}{4}) = (a_1', \dots, a_n')$ satisfies $a_1' = 2 = a_2'$.
So $f(\frac{a_1 a_2}{4}) \notin \Gamma_n$ and hence $\frac{a_1 a_2}{4} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$ by \eqref{9876543erfcnbvc9x87654}.
More generally, the same argument shows that
\begin{equation}  \label {ZoiugvXEWXzfvWbYHuyt9nJd8r763bncnAt7}
U_2 \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B) .
\end{equation}

Let $d \in M(B)$; since $M(B) \subseteq D$, $f(d) = (a_1', \dots, a_n')$ is defined and (by \eqref{9876543erfcnbvc9x87654}) does not belong to $\Gamma_n$;
so one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerata}
\item $a_i' = 1$ for some $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$,
\item $a_i' = 2 = a_j'$ for some distinct $i,j \in \{1,\dots,n\}$.
\end{enumerata}

Suppose that (a) holds.
Then \eqref{6gvhb3ag2n60b6tm9rn83h76b54} implies that $\gcd(a_i,L_i)=1$ (so $i \in I_1$ and $a_i \in U_1$)
and $\frac L{L_i} = \gcd( d , \frac L{L_i} )$, so $\frac L{L_i} \mid d$.
We have $\frac L{L_i} = a_i$ by \eqref{7236yhwebdcv5172wu}, so $a_i \mid d$ and hence $d \preceq a_i$.
We have $a_i \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$ by \eqref{987432sdxcpo09287h6hxcve} and $d$ is a maximal element of $(	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B),\preceq)$, so $d=a_i \in U_1$.
So if (a) holds then $d \in U_1$.

Suppose that (b) holds; here, we might as well assume that $a_1' = 2 = a_2'$.
Since $a_i' \mid a_i$ for all $i$, we see that $a_1$ and $a_2$ are even.
Since $a_1 \mid L_2$ and $a_2 \mid L_1$, both $L_1,L_2$ are even, so $\gcd(a_i,L_i)$ is even for $i=1,2$.
By \eqref{6gvhb3ag2n60b6tm9rn83h76b54}, we obtain that for each $i =1,2$, $\gcd(a_i,L_i) = 2$  and $\frac L{L_i} = \gcd( d , \frac L{L_i} )$, and hence $\frac L{L_i} \mid d$.
It also follows that $1,2 \in I_2$, so $\frac{a_1 a_2}4 \in U_2$ and $\frac{a_1 a_2}4 \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$ by \eqref{ZoiugvXEWXzfvWbYHuyt9nJd8r763bncnAt7}.
Since $\gcd( \frac L{L_1} , \frac L{L_2} ) = 1$ and (by \eqref{7236yhwebdcv5172wu}) $\frac L{L_i} = \frac{a_i}2$ for $i=1,2$,
we have $\frac{a_1 a_2}4 \mid d$ and hence $M(B) \ni d \preceq \frac{a_1 a_2}4 \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$, which implies that $d = \frac{a_1 a_2}4 \in U_2$.
So if (b) holds then $d \in U_2$.
This proves the first inclusion in:
$$
M(B) \subseteq U_1 \cup U_2 \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B) 
$$
where the second inclusion follows from \eqref{987432sdxcpo09287h6hxcve} and \eqref{ZoiugvXEWXzfvWbYHuyt9nJd8r763bncnAt7}.
If we set $t_i = a_i$ for $i \in I_1$ and $t_i = \frac{a_i}2$ for $i \in I_2$, then $t_i = \frac{L}{L_i}$ for all $i \in I_1 \cup I_2$, so
\begin{equation} \label {654edvbnmki87654esdcvbnhy543}
\text{the family $\big( t_i \big)_{i \in I_1 \cup I_2}$ is pairwise relatively prime}
\end{equation} 
by Lemma \ref{o8y7t626rf53deg23489jru3sgbref6}(a). 
Clearly,
\begin{equation} \label {bvcde45676543wsxcvbhuy6567ujnbxsw2}
U_1 = \big\{\, t_i \, \mid \, i \in I_1 \, \big\}  \quad \text{and} \quad  U_2 = \big\{\, t_j t_k \, \mid \, j,k \in I_2 \text{ and } j \neq k\, \big\} .
\end{equation}
Also note that $t_i>1$ for all $i \in I_1$, and that for $i \in I_2$ we have $t_i = 1$ $\Leftrightarrow$ $i=i_0$ (where $i_0$ is defined in the statement of the Proposition).

We will now use the following (easily verified) fact: {\it if $M(B) \subseteq P \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$ and $P$ is a primitive set, then $M(B)=P$.}

Assume that $i_0$ does not exist. Then $t_i>1$ for all $i \in I_1\cup I_2$, so \eqref{654edvbnmki87654esdcvbnhy543} and \eqref{bvcde45676543wsxcvbhuy6567ujnbxsw2}
imply that $U_1 \cup U_2$ is primitive. Since $M(B) \subseteq U_1 \cup U_2 \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$, we have $M(B)=U_1 \cup U_2$ in this case, as desired.

Assume that $i_0$ exists. Then $i_0 \in I_2$ and $t_{i_0}=1$.
For each $i \in I_2 \setminus \{i_0\}$ we have $t_i = t_{i_0}t_i \in U_2$; so $W \subseteq U_2 \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$, where we define $W = \big\{\, t_i \, \mid \, i \in I_2 \setminus \{i_0\} \, \big\}$.
Moreover, each element of $U_2 \setminus W$ is a product of two elements of $W$.
This implies that $M(B) \cap (U_2 \setminus W) = \varnothing$, because no element of $M(B)$ has a proper divisor that belongs to $	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$.
So $M(B) \subseteq U_1 \cup W \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$.
Since the elements of $U_1 \cup W$ $ = \big\{\, t_i \, \mid \, i \in I_1 \cup I_2 \setminus \{i_0\} \, \big\}$ are pairwise relatively prime and strictly larger than $1$,
$U_1 \cup W$ is primitive. So $M(B) = U_1 \cup W$, as desired.

title: Corollary
body_md:
\label {8bcnc4n57xdklidsocmo77456}
Let $m,n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ be such that $n\ge3$ and $0 \le m \le n-2$.
Let $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_n \ge2$ be pairwise relatively prime integers such that $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_m$ are odd.
Let $B = B_{ \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}; \ell_1, \dots, \ell_m, 2\ell_{m+1}, \dots, 2\ell_n }$.
Then 
$$
M(B) = \{ \ell_1, \dots, \ell_m \} \cup \big\{\, \ell_j \ell_k \, \mid \, m+1 \le j < k \le n \, \big\} .
$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $B = B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}; a_1, \dots, a_n}$ where $(a_1, \dots, a_n) = (\ell_1, \dots, \ell_m, 2\ell_{m+1}, \dots, 2\ell_n )$.
We have $L = 2 \prod_{i=1}^n \ell_i$ and the following hold for all $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$:
$$
\textstyle
\text{$L/L_i = \ell_i$ \quad and \quad
$\gcd(a_i,L_i) = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if $i \le m$,} \\ 2, & \text{if $i > m$.} \end{cases}$}
$$
We claim that $(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ satisfies assumption (ii) of Thm \ref{eion98h38dhb2d203ojfbdt7}.
Indeed, it is easy to see that if $d \in D$ then $f(d) = (\ell_1', \dots, \ell_m', 2\ell_{m+1}', \dots, 2\ell_n')$
where $\ell_i' \mid \ell_i$ for all $i=1,\dots,n$. It follows that $\ell_1', \dots, \ell_n'$ are pairwise relatively prime.
So, if $f(d) \in \Gamma_n$ then $	\operatorname{\text{\rm cotype}} f(d) \ge n-1$, so $B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}};f(d)}$ is rigid by Lemma \ref{4uygrfhejrFDfhgsdTHbfd68827djGD763}.
Thus, assumption (ii) of Thm \ref{eion98h38dhb2d203ojfbdt7} is satisfied.

In the notation of Thm \ref{eion98h38dhb2d203ojfbdt7}, we have $I_1 = \{1,\dots,m\}$, $I_2 = \{m+1, \dots, n\}$ and $i_0$ does not exist,
so $M(B) = \{ \ell_1, \dots, \ell_m \} \cup \big\{\, \ell_j \ell_k \, \mid \, m+1 \le j < k \le n \, \big\}$ by that result.

title: Proof
body_md:
If $Y = \varnothing$ then let $B = B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}};3,3,3}$.
We have $\bar e(B)=1$ by Lemma \ref{o8y7t626rf53deg23489jru3sgbref6}(b), 
so Cor.\ \ref{p98qy386e523brxhbfc6ghvc63x2345618q30} implies that $M(B)$ is either $\varnothing$ or $\{1\}$.
By $\mathscr{P}(3)$, $B$ is rigid, so  $1 \notin M(B)$ and hence $M(B) = \varnothing = Y$.

If $Y = \{1\}$ then let $B = B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}};1, 1, 1}$.  Since $B$ is non-rigid, $M(B) = \{1\} = Y$.

From now on, assume that $Y$ is neither $\varnothing$ nor $\{1\}$. Let $m = |Y| \ge 1$ and let $a_1, \dots, a_m$ be the 
distinct elements of $Y$. Then $a_1, \dots, a_m$ are pairwise relatively prime and $a_1, \dots, a_m \ge 2$.
Choose an integer $c\ge3$ such that  $a_1, \dots, a_m, c$ are pairwise relatively prime and let $B = B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}};a_1, \dots, a_m, c, c}$.

We claim that $(a_1,\dots,a_m,c,c)$ satisfies assumption (ii) of Thm \ref{eion98h38dhb2d203ojfbdt7}.
Indeed, it is easy to see that if $d \in D$ then $f(d) = (a_1',\dots,a_m',c,c)$ where $a_i' \mid a_i$ for all $i = 1,\dots,m$.
Note that $a_1', \dots, a_m', c$ are pairwise relatively prime.
If $f(d) \in \Gamma_{m+2}$ then $a_i'>1$ for all $i$, so $	\operatorname{\text{\rm cotype}}(a_1', \dots, a_m',c,c) = m$
and $B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}};a_1',\dots,a_m',c,c}$ is rigid by Lemma \ref{4uygrfhejrFDfhgsdTHbfd68827djGD763}.
Thus, assumption (ii) of Thm \ref{eion98h38dhb2d203ojfbdt7} is satisfied.

In the notation of Thm \ref{eion98h38dhb2d203ojfbdt7}, we have $I_1 = \{1, \dots, m\}$ and $I_2 = \varnothing$, so 
$M(B) =\{ a_1, \dots, a_m \} = Y$ by that result.

title: Notation
body_md:
Let $X$ be an integral scheme that is normal and noetherian.
Then we may consider the group $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Div}}(X)$ of Weil divisors of $X$, and the group $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Div}}_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}(X) = \ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}} \otimes_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Div}}(X)$ of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}$-divisors of $X$.
If $f$ is a nonzero element of the function field $K(X)$ of $X$ then the divisor of $f$ is denoted $	\operatorname{{\rm div}}_X(f)$;
so  $	\operatorname{{\rm div}}_X : K(X)^* \to 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Div}}(X)$ is a group homomorphism.

label: Pkcnbvc9w3eidjojf0q9w
body_md:
\label {Pkcnbvc9w3eidjojf0q9w}
(This is paragraph 5.4 in \cite{Chitayat-Daigle:cylindrical}, with minor edits.)
Let $B = \bigoplus_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}} B_i$ be an $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$-graded noetherian normal domain such that the prime ideal $B_+ = \bigoplus_{i > 0} B_i$
has height at least $2$.
Let $X = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}} B$ and $Y = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Proj}} B$, which are noetherian normal integral schemes.
We shall now define an injective $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}$-linear map $D \mapsto D^*$ from $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Div}}_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}(Y)$ to $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Div}}_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}(X)$.

Note that the function fields of $X$ and $Y$ satisfy $K(X) \supseteq K(Y)$.
Let $Y^{(1)}$ be the set of homogeneous prime ideals of $B$ of height $1$.
Since $	\operatorname{\text{\rm ht}}(B_+)>1$, each element of $Y^{(1)}$ is a point of $Y$; in fact we have $Y^{(1)} = \big\{\, y \in Y \, \mid \, \dim\EuScript{O}_{Y,y}=1 \, \big\}$.
For each ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Y^{(1)}$, $B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \supset B_{({\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})}$ is an extension of discrete valuation rings; let $e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ denote the ramification index of this extension.
Then $e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}\setminus \{0\}$.
If $v^Y_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} : K(Y)^* \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$ and 
$v^X_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} : K(X)^* \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$ denote the normalized\footnote{The word ``normalized'' means that the maps $v^Y_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ and $v^X_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ are surjective.}
valuations of $B_{({\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})}$ and $B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ respectively,
then $v^X_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} (\xi) = e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} v^Y_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}(\xi)$ for all $\xi \in K(Y)^*$.
Let $C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^Y$ (resp.~$C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^X$) denote the closure of $\{ {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \}$ in $Y$ (resp.\ in $X$).
Then $C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^Y$ (resp.~$C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^X$) is a prime divisor of $Y$ (resp.\ of $X$),
and every prime divisor of $Y$ is a $C^Y_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ for some ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Y^{(1)}$.
We define $( C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^Y )^* = e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^X$ for each ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Y^{(1)}$,
and extend linearly to  a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}$-linear map $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Div}}_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}(Y) \to 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Div}}_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}(X)$, $D \mapsto D^*$.
It is not hard to see that the linear map $D \mapsto D^*$ is injective and has the following property:
\begin{equation}
\label {PWSoidbfci27wyd}
\text{\it  $\big( 	\operatorname{{\rm div}}_Y(\xi) \big)^* = 	\operatorname{{\rm div}}_X(\xi)$ for all $\xi \in K(Y)^*$.}
\end{equation}

label: 7267e23ro98ifwhe8hfwjd
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) As $B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ is a discrete valuation ring and hence a principal ideal domain, there exists $g \in {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ such that ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} = g B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$.
We have to show that $g$ can be chosen to be homogeneous.
Note that $v^X_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}(g) = 1$.
Write $g = \sum_{i \in I} g_i$ where $I$ is a finite subset of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ and $g_i \in B_i \setminus \{0\}$ for all $i \in I$.
Since $g \in {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$, we have $g_i \in {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ and hence $v^X_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}(g_i) \ge 1$ for all $i \in I$.
If $v^X_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}(g_i) > 1$ for all $i \in I$ then $v^X_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}(g) > 1$, which is not the case.
So there exists $i \in I$ such that  $v^X_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}(g_i) = 1$. Then  ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} = g_i B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$, which proves (a).

Before proving (b), we show that
\begin{equation}  \label {ikjhhgcgrd6widcjb9wvcr}
\begin{minipage}{.8\textwidth}
If $x,y \in B \setminus \{0\}$ are homogeneous with $x/y \in B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^*$, then there exist homogeneous
$\alpha, \beta \in B \setminus {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ such that $x/y = \alpha/\beta$.
\end{minipage}
\end{equation}
To see this, we first choose $u \in B$ and $v \in B \setminus {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ such that $x/y = u/v$.
Write $u = \sum_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}} u_i$ and $v = \sum_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}} v_i$ where $u_i,v_i \in B_i$ for all $i$,
and choose $j \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} $ such that $v_j \in B_j \setminus {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$.
Then the equality $x\sum_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}} v_i = y \sum_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}} u_i$ implies that $xv_j = y u_i$ for some $i$.
So $x/y = u_i / v_j$. If $u_i \in {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ then $u_i/v_j$ belongs to ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$, contradicting $x/y \in B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^*$.
So $u_i \in B_i \setminus {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$, which proves \eqref{ikjhhgcgrd6widcjb9wvcr}.

(b) Let $g$ be a homogeneous element of ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ such that  ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} = g B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$. 
Let $\delta = \gcd( \deg(g), e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}))$.
Pick any $i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ such that $B_i \neq 0$ and pick $h \in B_i \setminus \{0\}$.
For some $\nu \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$, we have $h/g^\nu \in B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^*$;
so \eqref{ikjhhgcgrd6widcjb9wvcr} implies that $h/g^\nu = \alpha/\beta$ for some homogeneous $\alpha,\beta \in B \setminus {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$.
Then $\delta \mid e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \mid \deg(\gamma)$ for each $\gamma \in \{\alpha,\beta\}$.
We have $\deg(h) - \nu \deg(g) = \deg(\alpha) - \deg(\beta)$, so $\delta$ divides $\deg(h) = i$.
This being true for each $i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ such that $B_i \neq0$, we conclude that $\delta \mid e(B)$.
Clearly, $e(B) \mid \delta$; so (b) is true. 


(c) Let $g$ be as in (a) and (b).
Let $\varepsilon = e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})$ and $d = e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})/e(B) = \varepsilon/e(B)$.
Since $e(B) \mid \deg(g)$,
$\deg(g^d)$ belongs to $\varepsilon \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$, which is the group generated by $\big\{\, i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} \, \mid \, (B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})_i \neq 0 \, \big\}$;
so there exist $i,j \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ such that $(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})_i \neq 0$,  $(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})_j \neq 0$, and $\deg(g^d) = i-j$;
consequently, there exist homogeneous elements $u,v \in B \setminus {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ such that $\deg(g^d) = \deg(v) - \deg(u)$.
Then $\xi = g^d u / v $ belongs to the maximal ideal ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{m}}}$ of $B_{({\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})}$.
Let us prove that ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{m}}} = \xi B_{({\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})}$.

Consider an arbitrary nonzero element $\frac xs$ of ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{m}}}$, where $x,s \in B \setminus \{0\}$ are homogeneous of the same degree and $s \notin {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$. 
Define  $k = v^X_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}\big( \frac xs \big)$.
Then $k>0$, because $\frac xs \in {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{m}}} \subseteq {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$; it follows that $\frac{x}{sg^k} \in B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^*$,
so \eqref{ikjhhgcgrd6widcjb9wvcr} implies that $\frac{x}{sg^k} = \frac{b_m}{c_\ell}$ for some
$b_m \in B_m \setminus {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ and $c_\ell \in B_\ell \setminus {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$.
Since  $c_\ell, b_m \in B \setminus {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$, we have $\ell, m \in \varepsilon\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$.
Since  $\frac xs = g^k \frac{b_m}{c_\ell}$, we have $k \deg(g) + m - \ell = \deg(x) - \deg(s) = 0$;
it follows that $\varepsilon \mid k \deg(g)$, or equivalently, $d \mid k \frac{\deg(g)}{e(B)}$.
Part (b) shows that $d = \frac{\varepsilon}{e(B)}$ is relatively prime to $\frac{\deg(g)}{e(B)}$, so $d \mid k$.
Write $k = k_0 d$ (where $k_0>0$), then 
$$
\frac xs = g^{k_0 d} \, \frac{b_m}{c_\ell} 
= \left(g^{d} \frac uv\right)^{k_0} \frac{v^{k_0}b_m}{u^{k_0}c_\ell} 
= \xi^{k_0} \frac{v^{k_0}b_m}{u^{k_0}c_\ell} 
$$
where $\frac{v^{k_0}b_m}{u^{k_0}c_\ell} \in B_{({\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})}^*$.
Since $k_0>0$, we have $\frac xs \in \xi B_{({\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})}$, which shows that ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{m}}} = \xi B_{({\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})}$.
Consequently, $e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} = v^X_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}( \xi ) = v^X_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}(  g^d u / v ) = d$, which proves (c).

Let the assumptions and notations be as in paragraph \ref{Pkcnbvc9w3eidjojf0q9w}.
Then $B$ is saturated in codimension $1$ if and only if $e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} = 1$ for all ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Y^{(1)}$.

body_md:
\label {7tyzvcxzcvbcvQcksbvcstdio976543dfsxnbx48}
{\bf Proof of Theorem \ref{jh782uwsdvvhjkqw547182}.}
Part (b) is well known.
In part (a), the fact that $\Delta$ exists, is unique, and is an ample $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}$-divisor was proved in \cite[Thm 3.5]{Demazure_1988}.
Assertion (a-ii) is well known (see for instance  \cite[5.20(a)]{Chitayat-Daigle:cylindrical}), and (a-iii) follows from \cite[Cor.\ 5.20(d)]{Chitayat-Daigle:cylindrical}.
Let us prove (a-iv).
The article \cite{Demazure_1988} explains how to compute $\Delta$ from the given $t$, but it is easier to use the statement of \cite[Thm 5.9]{Chitayat-Daigle:cylindrical},
which asserts that $\Delta^* = 	\operatorname{{\rm div}}_X(t)$.
By definition of the injective map $D \mapsto D^*$ (see \ref{Pkcnbvc9w3eidjojf0q9w}), this gives the first equality in:
$$
\textstyle
\Delta
= \sum_{ {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Y^{(1)} } \frac{ v_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^X(t) }{ e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} }  C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^Y 
= \sum_{ {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Y^{(1)} } \frac{ v_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^X(t) }{ e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) }  C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^Y , 
$$
where the second equality follows from the assumption $e(B)=1$ together with part (c) of Lemma \ref{7267e23ro98ifwhe8hfwjd}.
So $\Delta \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Div}}(Y)$ if and only if
\begin{equation}  \label {8A32uCyifbPMk8590mNBEWw6289}
\text{$e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \mid v_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^X(t)$ \ \  for all ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Y^{(1)}$.}
\end{equation}
Let ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Y^{(1)}$.
By Lemma \ref{7267e23ro98ifwhe8hfwjd}(a), there exists a homogeneous element $g$ of ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ such that ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} = g B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$.
Let $\nu = v_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^X(t)$ and note that $t/g^\nu \in B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^*$;
by \eqref{ikjhhgcgrd6widcjb9wvcr}, we have $t/g^\nu = \alpha/\beta$ for some homogeneous $\alpha,\beta \in B \setminus {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$.
Since $1 = \deg(t) = \nu \deg(g) + \deg(\alpha) - \deg(\beta)$ and $e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})$ divides $\deg(\alpha)$  and $\deg(\beta)$,
$e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})$ is relatively prime to $\nu =v_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^X(t)$.
This being true for each ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Y^{(1)}$, we obtain that
\eqref{8A32uCyifbPMk8590mNBEWw6289} is equivalent to $e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})=1$ for all ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Y^{(1)}$,
which is itself equivalent to $B$ being saturated in codimension $1$.
This proves (a-iv), and completes the proof of Thm \ref{jh782uwsdvvhjkqw547182}.
\hfill\qedsymbol

body_md:
\label {iwyr8762367ds2wxfwd2w2f3rfvtm0m00}
Given an $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$-graded ring $A = \bigoplus_{ i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} } A_i$ and $d \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}\setminus \{0\}$, we define the $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$-graded ring
$A^{\langle d \rangle} = S = \bigoplus_{ i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} } S_i$ by setting $S_i = A_{di}$ for all $i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$.
Note that $A^{\langle d \rangle}$ and $A^{(d)}$ are the same ring, but have different gradings: if $x \in S_i \setminus \{0\}$
then $x$ is a homogeneous element of both $A^{\langle d \rangle}$ and $A^{(d)}$,
the degree of $x$ in $A^{\langle d \rangle}$ is $i$, and the degree of $x$ in $A^{(d)}$ is $di$.
Observe that $A^{(d)} \overset{\text{\tiny$*$}}{\cong} A^{\langle d \rangle}$, in the notation of \ref{98if9jvs9d772jfpd0vhf9w93uo0541hf9}.

\label {7654cvhgfsd2d34fds23f42dfdghjk8l}
Let ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and
$B = \bigoplus_{n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}} B_n$ an $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$-graded normal affine ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-domain
such that the prime ideal $B_+ = \bigoplus_{n > 0} B_n$ has height at least $2$.
Let $x$ be a homogeneous prime element of $B$ of degree $d>0$.
If $B_{(x)}$ is non-rigid then so is $(B/xB)^{(d)}$.

label: cjb738645q9mbr2hnbmadp28570
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $X = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}} B$ and $Y = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Proj}} B$, and let us use the notations of paragraph \ref{Pkcnbvc9w3eidjojf0q9w}
(this is why we need to assume that $	\operatorname{\text{\rm ht}}(B_+)\ge2$ in Thm \ref{7654cvhgfsd2d34fds23f42dfdghjk8l}).
Let ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} = xB \in Y^{(1)}$ and consider the valuations $v_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^X : K(X) \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \cup \{\infty\}$ and $v_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^Y : K(Y) \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \cup \{\infty\}$
and the  ramification index  $e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$.
Lemma \ref{7267e23ro98ifwhe8hfwjd} gives
\begin{equation}  \label {cjb738645q9mbr2hnbmadp28570}
\textstyle
\gcd(d, e(B/xB) ) = e(B) \quad \text{and} \quad e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}  = \frac{ e( B/xB ) }{ e(B) } .
\end{equation}

Consider $C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^Y \subset Y$ and $C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^X \subset X$ as in \ref{Pkcnbvc9w3eidjojf0q9w};
note that $C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^Y = \ensuremath{\mathbb{V}}_+(x) \subset Y$ and let $U = \ensuremath{\mathbb{D}}_+(x) = Y \setminus C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^Y$.
Let $R = B_{(x)}$ and note that $R$ is a subring of $K(Y)$.
We claim:
\begin{equation}  \label {E1nfo83aTcbpqc0gfrnxjg}
\text{if $f \in R \setminus \{0\}$ then $	\operatorname{{\rm div}}_U(f) \ge 0$  and  $v_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^Y(f) \le 0$.}
\end{equation}
Indeed, for each ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{q}}} \in Y^{(1)} \setminus \{{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}\}$, we have $R = B_{(x)} \subseteq B_{({\ensuremath{\mathfrak{q}}})}$ and hence $v_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{q}}}^Y(f) \ge0$; so $	\operatorname{{\rm div}}_U(f) \ge 0$.
Since $f \in R \setminus \{0\}$, we have $f = g/x^n$ for some $n \ge 0$ and $g \in B_{nd} \setminus \{0\}$.
If $v_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^Y(f) > 0$ then $f = xb/s$ where $b \in B \setminus \{0\}$ and $s \in B \setminus {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ are homogeneous and $\deg(xb) = \deg(s)$;
then $g/x^n = xb/s$, so $x^{n+1} \mid sg$; since $x$ is prime and $x \nmid s$ in $B$, we obtain $x^{n+1} \mid g$, which contradicts $g \in B_{nd} \setminus \{0\}$.
So \eqref{E1nfo83aTcbpqc0gfrnxjg} is true.
Consequently, the map
$$
\deg_R : R \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} \cup \{ - \infty \}, \quad \text{$\deg_R(f) = -v_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^Y(f)$ for all $f \in R$}
$$
is a well-defined  degree function.
Consider the associated graded ring $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Gr}}(R)$ determined by $(R,\deg_R)$;
recall that $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Gr}}(R) = \bigoplus_{n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}} R_{\le n} / R_{<n}$ where for each $n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ we set
$$
R_{\le n} = \big\{\, r \in R \, \mid \, \deg_R(r) \le n \, \big\} \quad \text{and} \quad R_{< n} = \big\{\, r \in R \, \mid \, \deg_R(r) < n \, \big\} \quad \text{(so $R_{<0} = 0 $).}
$$
Since $v_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^Y : K(Y) \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \cup \{\infty\}$ is surjective and $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Frac}} R = K(Y)$, it follows that $e( 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Gr}} R ) = 1$.
We claim (see Notation \ref{iwyr8762367ds2wxfwd2w2f3rfvtm0m00}):
\begin{equation}  \label {765wjwejnbfcx67678o}
	\operatorname{\text{\rm Gr}}(R) \cong \big( B/x B \big)^{\langle e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} d \rangle} .
\end{equation}
Let us prove \eqref{765wjwejnbfcx67678o}.
Given $f \in R \setminus \{0\}$, let $S(f) = \big\{\, n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} \, \mid \, f x^n \in B \, \big\}$ and note that $S(f)$ is a nonempty subset of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$.
Clearly, if $n \in S(f)$ then $n+1 \in S(f)$.
We claim that 
\begin{equation}  \label {A87tr7ghcjomgIbbvncvnsuieruo3834}
\text{for each $f \in R \setminus \{0\}$,} \quad S(f) = \big\{\, n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} \, \mid \, n \ge e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \deg_R(f) \, \big\} .
\end{equation}
Indeed, let $f \in R \setminus \{0\}$. Given any $n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$, we have
$n \in S(f) \iff f x^n \in B \iff 	\operatorname{{\rm div}}_X(f x^n) \ge 0$.
Consider the $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}$-linear map $D \mapsto D^*$ from $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Div}}_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}(Y)$ to $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Div}}_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}(X)$ defined in \ref{Pkcnbvc9w3eidjojf0q9w};
then $(C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^Y )^* = {e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}} C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^X$, and \eqref{PWSoidbfci27wyd} gives $( 	\operatorname{{\rm div}}_Y(f))^* = 	\operatorname{{\rm div}}_X(f)$.
Since 
$$
\textstyle
	\operatorname{{\rm div}}_X(f x^n) 
= 	\operatorname{{\rm div}}_X(f) + n 	\operatorname{{\rm div}}_X(x)
= 	\operatorname{{\rm div}}_X(f) + n C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^X
= ( 	\operatorname{{\rm div}}_Y(f) + \frac n{e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}} C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^Y )^*,
$$
and since $D^* \ge0 \Leftrightarrow D \ge 0$ for any $D \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Div}}_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}(Y)$,
we have
\begin{equation*}  
\textstyle
n \in S(f) \iff 	\operatorname{{\rm div}}_Y(f) +  \frac n{e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}} C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^Y  \ge 0
\iff v_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^Y(f) \ge -\frac n{e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}} \iff \deg_R(f) \le \frac n{e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}},
\end{equation*}
where the middle equivalence follows from $	\operatorname{{\rm div}}_U(f) \ge 0$ (see \eqref{E1nfo83aTcbpqc0gfrnxjg}).
This proves \eqref{A87tr7ghcjomgIbbvncvnsuieruo3834}.
Now \eqref{A87tr7ghcjomgIbbvncvnsuieruo3834} implies that if $n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ and $f \in R \setminus \{0\}$ then:
\begin{align*}
f \in R_{\le n} & \Leftrightarrow \deg_R(f) \le n \Leftrightarrow e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} n \in S(f) \Leftrightarrow f x^{e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} n} \in B ; \\
f \in R_{< n} & \Leftrightarrow \deg_R(f) < n \Leftrightarrow e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} n > \min S(f) \Leftrightarrow  e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} n - 1 \in S(f)
\Leftrightarrow  f x^{e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} n - 1} \in B \\
& \Leftrightarrow  f x^{e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} n } \in xB.
\end{align*}
So the following holds for each $n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$:
\begin{equation*} 
\text{each $f \in R_{\le n}$ satisfies\ \ $\big( f x^{e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} n} \in B$\ \ and\ \  $f x^{e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} n} \in xB \Leftrightarrow f \in R_{< n}\big)$.}
\end{equation*}
So, for each $n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$, the ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-linear map $\theta_n :R_{\le n} \to B_{d e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} n}$, $f \mapsto f x^{e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} n}$, 
is well-defined and induces an injective ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-linear map $\bar\theta_n :  R_{\le n} / R_{<n} \to (B/xB)_{d e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} n}$. 
Note that $\bar\theta_n$ is also surjective.
Indeed, consider $\xi \in (B/xB)_{d e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} n}$. 
Then $\xi = h + xB$ for some $h \in B_{d e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} n}$. 
Obviously, if $h=0$ then $\xi \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm im}}( \bar\theta_n )$.
Assume that $h \neq0$ and let $f = h/x^{e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} n} \in R \setminus \{0\}$;
then $e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} n \in S(f)$ by definition of $S(f)$, so $e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} n \ge e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \deg_R(f)$ by \eqref{A87tr7ghcjomgIbbvncvnsuieruo3834}, so $\deg_R(f) \le n$,
i.e., $f \in R_{\le n}$; we have $\theta_n(f) = h$, so $\bar\theta_n( f + R_{<n} ) = \xi$.
This shows that, for each $n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$, the ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-linear map  $\bar\theta_n :  R_{\le n} / R_{<n} \to (B/xB)_{d e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} n}$ is bijective.
The family $\big(\bar\theta_n \big)_{ n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} }$ defines an injective ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-linear map $\bar\theta : 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Gr}}(R) \to B/xB$
which is easily seen to preserve multiplication. Moreover, the image of $\bar\theta$ is the subring $\big( B/xB )^{(d e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} )}$ of $B/xB$.
If we define $S_n =  (B/xB)_{d e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} n}$ for all $n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$, then $\big( B/xB )^{ \langle d e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \rangle } = \bigoplus_{n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}} S_n$,
so $\bar\theta : 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Gr}}(R) \to \big( B/xB )^{ \langle d e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \rangle }$
is a degree-preserving isomorphism of graded ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-algebras. 
This proves \eqref{765wjwejnbfcx67678o}.


It follows from \eqref{765wjwejnbfcx67678o} that $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Gr}}(R)$ is ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-affine
(because $( B/x B \big)^{\langle d e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \rangle}$ is ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-affine by Cor.\ \ref{8Qp98781hy2uexihvcx2qw2wUxq3ew0pokjmnbvaw2345}),
so part (b) of Theorem 1.7 of \cite{Dai:TameWild}
implies that $\deg_R$ is tame over ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ (in the terminology of \cite{Dai:TameWild}, this means that 
for every ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-derivation $D : R \to R$, the set $\big\{\, \deg_R( Dr ) - \deg_R(r) \, \mid \, r \in R \setminus \{0\} \, \big\}$ has a greatest element).
As is well known, this implies that each element $D$ of $	\operatorname{\text{\rm LND}}(R) \setminus \{0\}$ gives rise to a well-defined $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Gr}}(D) : 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Gr}}(R) \to 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Gr}}(R)$
which belongs to $	\operatorname{\text{\rm HLND}}( 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Gr}} R ) \setminus \{0\}$.
So if $	\operatorname{\text{\rm LND}}(R) \neq \{0\}$ then $	\operatorname{\text{\rm HLND}}( 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Gr}} R ) \neq \{0\}$,
which (by \eqref{765wjwejnbfcx67678o}) implies $	\operatorname{\text{\rm HLND}}\big( \big( B/x B \big)^{\langle d e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \rangle} \big) \neq \{0\}$, 
which implies that $\big( B/x B \big)^{\langle d e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \rangle}$ is non-rigid. 
Since the graded rings $\big( B/x B \big)^{\langle d e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \rangle}$ and $\big( B/x B \big)^{( d e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} )}$ have the same underlying ring,
and since (by definition) rigidity only depends on the underlying ring, we have shown that 
\begin{equation}  \label {u765r0x9id21wsxyud56rb75v2ubvcexzLu504odkUT3}
\text{if $R = B_{(x)}$ is non-rigid then $\big( B/x B \big)^{( d e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} )}$ is non-rigid}.
\end{equation}
By Cor.\ \ref{mMpPiq13096gxvbw5resip0tfs}(a) and \eqref{cjb738645q9mbr2hnbmadp28570},
$e\big( (B/xB)^{(d)} \big) = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}(d, e(B/xB) ) = \frac{ d \, e(B/xB) }{ e(B) } = d e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$,
which implies that $(B/xB)^{(d)} = (B/xB)^{(d e_{{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}})}$.
This together with \eqref{u765r0x9id21wsxyud56rb75v2ubvcexzLu504odkUT3} completes the proof.

label: 9879686754evcxyui9q
title: Proof
body_md:
We may assume that $i=n$, so it suffices to prove that 
$$
\text{\it if $S({\mathbf{a}}) \subseteq \{n\}$ and $(B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}} })_{(x_n)}$ is non-rigid, then $B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}}(n) }$ is non-rigid.}
$$
Suppose that $S({\mathbf{a}}) \subseteq \{n\}$ and that $(B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}} })_{(x_n)}$ is non-rigid.
Thm \ref{7654cvhgfsd2d34fds23f42dfdghjk8l} implies that $( B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}} } / x_n B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}} } )^{(d_n)}$ is non-rigid.
Note that $B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}} } / x_n B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}} } \overset{\text{\tiny$*$}}{\cong} B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}}(n) }$ (see Notation \ref{98if9jvs9d772jfpd0vhf9w93uo0541hf9});
we claim:
\begin{equation}  \label {9879686754evcxyui9q}
\big( B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}} } / x_n B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}} } \big)^{(d_n)} \overset{\text{\tiny$*$}}{\cong} \big( B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}}(n) } \big)^{(d_n)} .
\end{equation}
This has to be carefully argued, because in general the condition $A \overset{\text{\tiny$*$}}{\cong} B$ does not imply that $A^{(d)} \overset{\text{\tiny$*$}}{\cong} B^{(d)}$ for all $d$.\footnote{For instance,
let $A = {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}[X_1,X_2] = {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}^{[{2}]}$ and $B = {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}[Y_1,Y_2] = {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}^{[{2}]}$ where $\deg(X_i)=1$ and $\deg(Y_i)=2$.
Then $A \overset{\text{\tiny$*$}}{\cong} B$ is true but $A^{(2)} \overset{\text{\tiny$*$}}{\cong} B^{(2)}$ is false, as $B^{(2)} = B$ is a polynomial ring but $A^{(2)}$ is not.}
If we use the notations $\bar B =B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}} } / x_n B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}} }$, $C = B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}}(n) }$ and $\varepsilon = \gcd(d_1,\dots,d_{n-1})$,
then $e(\bar B) = \varepsilon$
and there is an isomorphism of ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-algebras $\varphi : \bar B \to C$ satisfying:
$$
\varphi( \bar B_{i} ) = \begin{cases}
C_{i/\varepsilon} & \text{if $i \in \varepsilon\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$,} \\
0 & \text{if $i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} \setminus \varepsilon\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$.}
\end{cases}
$$
Let $\ell = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}(\varepsilon,d_n)$; then $e( \bar B^{(d_n)} ) = \ell$ by Cor.\ \ref{mMpPiq13096gxvbw5resip0tfs}(a), so $\bar B^{(d_n)} = \bar B^{(\ell)}$ and hence
$$
\textstyle
\varphi\big( \bar B^{(d_n)} \big)
= \varphi\big( \bar B^{( \ell )} \big)
= \varphi\big( \bigoplus_{ i \in \ell\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} } \bar B_{i} \big)
= \bigoplus_{ i \in \ell\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} } C_{i/\varepsilon}
= \bigoplus_{ j \in (\ell/\varepsilon)\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} } C_{j} = C^{( \ell/\varepsilon )} ,
$$
showing that $( \bar B )^{(d_n)} \overset{\text{\tiny$*$}}{\cong} C^{(\ell/\varepsilon)}$.
Since $\gcd(\varepsilon,d_n) = \gcd(d_1, \dots, d_n) = 1$, we have $\ell/\varepsilon = d_n$,
so $( \bar B )^{(d_n)} \overset{\text{\tiny$*$}}{\cong} C^{(d_n)}$.  This proves \eqref{9879686754evcxyui9q}.
Next, we prove:
\begin{equation}  \label {i76f5de4ws0A0olciunmnbvce231zx9}
\gcd( d_n , \bar e(B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}}(n) }) ) = 1 .
\end{equation}
We have $\bar e(B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}}(n) }) = \prod_{j=1}^{n-1} \frac{	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}(a_1,\dots,a_{n-1})}{	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}(a_1,\dots, \widehat{a_j} , \dots, a_{n-1})}$
by Lemma \ref{o8y7t626rf53deg23489jru3sgbref6}.
Suppose that $p$ is a prime number that divides both $d_n$ and $\bar e(B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}}(n) })$.
Since $p \mid \prod_{j=1}^{n-1} \frac{	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}(a_1,\dots,a_{n-1})}{	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}(a_1,\dots, \widehat{a_j} , \dots, a_{n-1})}$,
there exists $j \in \{1,\dots,n-1\}$ such that $v_p(a_j) >  \max( v_p(a_1) , \dots, \widehat{ v_p(a_j) } , \dots, v_p(a_{n-1}) )$.
Since $p$ divides $d_n = L/a_n$, we have $v_p(a_n) < \max( v_p(a_1) , \dots, v_p(a_{n-1}) ) = v_p(a_j)$, so
$v_p(a_j) >  \max( v_p(a_1) , \dots, \widehat{ v_p(a_j) } , \dots, v_p(a_{n}) ) = v_p( L_j )$.
It follows that $v_p(L) \ge v_p(a_j) > v_p( L_j )$, so $j \in S({\mathbf{a}})$, which contradicts $S({\mathbf{a}}) \subseteq \{n\}$.
So $p$ does not exist, and this proves \eqref{i76f5de4ws0A0olciunmnbvce231zx9}.



Since $\big( B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}} } / x_n B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}} } \big)^{(d_n)}$ is non-rigid,
\eqref{9879686754evcxyui9q} implies that $(B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}}(n) })^{(d_n)}$ is non-rigid.
Thus, $d_n \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}( B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}}(n) } ) = \bigcup_{ d \in M( B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}}(n) } ) } \mathscr{I}_d$,
where the equality is Cor.\ \ref{p98qy386e523brxhbfc6ghvc63x2345618q30}(a).
It follows that there exists $d \in M( B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}}(n) } )$ such that $d \mid d_n$.
Cor.\ \ref{p98qy386e523brxhbfc6ghvc63x2345618q30}(b) gives $d \mid \bar e(B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}}(n) })$,
so $d=1$ by \eqref{i76f5de4ws0A0olciunmnbvce231zx9}.
This means that $1 \in M( B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}}(n) } )$, so $B_{ {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} ; {\mathbf{a}}(n) }$ is non-rigid, as desired.

body_md:

Let ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ be an algebraically closed field, $n\ge1$ and $F \in A = {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}^{[{n}]}$. Then the set
$ \big\{\, \lambda \in {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} \, \mid \, \text{$F-\lambda$ is not irreducible in $A$} \, \big\} $
is either finite or equal to ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$, and it is equal to ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ if and only if
$F = P(G)$ for some $G \in A$ and some univariate polynomial $P(T) \in {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}[T]$
such that $\deg_T P(T) > 1$.

Let ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ be a field of characteristic $0$, $\bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}$ an algebraic closure of ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$, $n\ge1$ and $R = {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}[X_1,\dots,X_n] = {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}^{[n]}$.
Endow $R$ with an $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$-grading such that each $X_i$ is homogeneous and let $f$ be a homogeneous prime element of $R$ of positive degree.
Then $f-\lambda$ is irreducible over $\bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}$ for every $\lambda \in \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}^*$.

label: 765432erghxdnjkrg67h8j90monk
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\bar R = \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}[X_1,\dots,X_n] = \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}^{[n]}$.
Let $m=\deg(f)>0$ and $d_i = \deg(X_i)$ ($1 \le i \le n$).
For each $\lambda \in \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}^*$, consider the $\bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}$-automorphism $\mu_\lambda$ of $\bar R$ defined by
$\mu_\lambda(X_i) = \lambda^{d_i} X_i$ ($1 \le i \le n$).
If $\lambda, \lambda_0 \in \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}^*$ then $\mu_\lambda( f - \lambda^m \lambda_0 ) = \lambda^m(f-\lambda_0)$,
so the $\bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}$-algebras $\bar R / (f - \lambda_0)$ and $\bar R / (f - \lambda^m \lambda_0)$ are isomorphic.
Since $m>0$, it follows that
\begin{equation}  \label {765432erghxdnjkrg67h8j90monk}
\text{for all $\lambda_1,\lambda_2 \in \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}^*$, \quad $\bar R / (f - \lambda_1)$ is $\bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}$-isomorphic to $\bar R / (f - \lambda_2)$.}
\end{equation}

Arguing by contradiction, suppose that $f-\lambda$ is reducible in $\bar R$, for some $\lambda \in \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}^*$.
Then, by \eqref{765432erghxdnjkrg67h8j90monk}, $f-\lambda$ is reducible in $\bar R$ for all $\lambda \in \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}^*$.
So Lemma \ref{Matsudp23rwije} implies that $f = P(g)$ for some $g \in \bar R$ and some univariate polynomial $P(T) \in \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}[T]$ such
that $\deg_T P(T) > 1$. Using that $f$ is homogeneous of positive degree, we see that $g$ may be chosen so as to have $P(T) = T^r$, where $r\ge2$.
Thus, $f = g^r$.
For each $\theta \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Gal}}(\bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}/{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}})$, define $\tilde\theta : \bar R \to \bar R$ as in Lemma \ref{cccy5hc7cnc8c4cg}.
Then $\tilde\theta(g)^r = f$, so $( \tilde\theta(g) / g )^r = 1$.
This shows that for each $\theta \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Gal}}(\bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}/{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}})$ there exists $\lambda_\theta \in \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}^*$ such that $\tilde\theta(g)=\lambda_\theta g$.
By Lemma \ref{cccy5hc7cnc8c4cg}, it follows that there exists $\lambda \in \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}^*$ such that $\lambda g \in R$.
So $f = (\lambda^{-r}) (\lambda g)^r$ is not irreducible in $R$, a contradiction.

label: 87t7weg5r237r8jwngbvcb37wj83y
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label {87t7weg5r237r8jwngbvcb37wj83y}
Let ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ be a field of characteristic $0$, $\bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}$ an algebraic closure of ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$, $n\ge2$,
and $f$ an irreducible element of $R = {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}[X_1, \dots, X_{n}] = {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}^{[{n}]}$.
Then the zero-set of $( f, \frac{\partial f}{\partial X_1}, \dots, \frac{\partial f}{\partial X_n} )$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{A}}^n_{ \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}} }$ has dimension
at most $n-2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If the conclusion is false then there exists a prime element $g$ of $\bar R = \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}[X_1, \dots, X_{n}]$ that is a common divisor
of $f$, $\frac{\partial f}{\partial X_1}$, \dots, $\frac{\partial f}{\partial X_n}$ in  $\bar R$.
Choose $i$ such that $\frac{\partial g}{\partial X_i} \neq 0$ and note that $\frac{\partial f}{\partial X_i} \neq 0$.
Let $K = {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}(X_1, \dots, \widehat{X_i}, \dots, X_n)$ and $\bar K = \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}(X_1, \dots, \widehat{X_i}, \dots, X_n)$.
Note that $f$ (resp.\ $g$) is an irreducible element of $K[X_i] = K^{[1]}$ (resp.\  of $\bar K[X_i] = \bar K^{[1]}$).
It follows that $\gcd( f, \frac{\partial f}{\partial X_i}) = 1$ in $K[X_i]$, so $uf+v \frac{\partial f}{\partial X_i} = 1$ for some $u,v \in K[X_i]$,
so $\gcd( f, \frac{\partial f}{\partial X_i}) = 1$ in $\bar K[X_i]$, contradicting the fact that $g$ is 
an irreducible element of $\bar K[X_i]$ that divides both $f$ and $\frac{\partial f}{\partial X_i}$.

label: u65vmklio909543qsdfh4vue
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $S := R/fR = \bigoplus_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}}S_i$ is an $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$-graded domain, $S^* = S_0^*$.
The fact that $\deg(f)>0$ implies that $S_0 = R_0$, and we have $R_0 = {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}^{[{r}]}$ for some $r\ge0$, so $S^* = S_0^* = R_0^* = {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}^*$,
i.e., $R/fR$ has trivial units. So the case $c=0$ of (a) is true.
Obviously, the case $c=0$ of (b) is also true. 

Until the end of the proof, we assume that $c \in {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}^*$.
Lemma \ref{9823bSnby5is5wckdsohf} implies that $R/(f-c)$ is a domain.
To complete the proof of the Proposition, it remains to show that $R/(f-c)$ has trivial units, and that if $R/fR$ is rigid then so is $R/(f-c)$.

Let $m=\deg(f)>0$ and $d_i = \deg(X_i) \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ ($1 \le i \le n$).
We claim that $f - c X_{n+1}^m$ is irreducible in $\bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}[X_1, \dots, X_{n+1}] = \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}^{[n+1]}$, where  $\bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}$ is an algebraic closure of ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$.
Indeed, suppose that $G,H \in \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}[X_1, \dots, X_{n+1}]$ are such that $f - c X_{n+1}^m = GH$.
For each $\lambda \in \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}^*$, define $G(\lambda) = G(X_1,\dots,X_n,\lambda)$ and $H(\lambda) = H(X_1,\dots,X_n,\lambda)$.
Then for each $\lambda \in \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}^*$ we have  $f - c \lambda^m = G(\lambda)H(\lambda)$.
Since $f - c \lambda^m$ is irreducible over $\bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}$ by Lemma \ref{9823bSnby5is5wckdsohf},
it follows that  $G(\lambda)\in \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}^*$ or $H(\lambda)\in\bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}^*$.
So there exists $W \in \{G,H\}$ such that $W(\lambda)\in \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}^*$ is true for infinitely many $\lambda \in \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}$.
This implies that $W \in \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}[ X_{n+1}]$.
There exists $V \in \{G,H\}$ such that  $WV = f-cX_{n+1}^m$;
pick $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ such that $\frac{\partial f}{\partial X_i} \neq 0$, then 
$W\frac{\partial V}{\partial X_i} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial X_i} \in {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}[X_1,\dots,X_n] \setminus \{0\}$ shows that $W \in \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}^*$,
which, in turn, shows that $f - c X_{n+1}^m$ is irreducible in $\bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}[X_1, \dots, X_{n+1}]$.
So both $B = {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}[X_1, \dots, X_{n+1}] / (f - c X_{n+1}^m)$ and $\bar B = \bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}} \otimes_{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} B$ are domains.

We claim that $B$ and $\bar B$ are normal. This is clear if $m=1$, so assume that $m\ge2$.
Then the singular locus of the affine variety $X = V(f - c X_{n+1}^m) \subset \ensuremath{\mathbb{A}}_{\bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}}^{n+1}$ 
is $V(X_{n+1}, f, \frac{\partial f}{\partial X_1}, \dots, \frac{\partial f}{\partial X_n} ) \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathbb{A}}_{\bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}}^{n+1}$.
By Lemma \ref{87t7weg5r237r8jwngbvcb37wj83y}, we see that the codimension of $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Sing}}(X)$ in $X$ is greater than $1$;
since $X$ is a hypersurface of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{A}}^{n+1}_{\bar{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}}}$, it follows that $X$ is normal. Since $X \cong 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}} \bar B$, $\bar B$ is normal.
It is well known that $\bar B \cap 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Frac}}(B) = B$, so $B$ is normal.


Define an $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$-grading on ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}[X_1, \dots, X_{n+1}]$ by declaring that $X_{n+1}$ is homogeneous of degree $1$
and (for $1 \le i \le n$) $X_i$ is homogeneous of degree $d_i$.
Then $f - c X_{n+1}^m$ is homogeneous, so $B$ is $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$-graded.
Write $B = {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}[x_1, \dots, x_{n+1}] = \bigoplus_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}} B_i$ where $x_i$ is the canonical image of $X_i$ in $B$.
Since $x_1$ and $x_{n+1}$ have positive degrees and are algebraically independent over $B_0$ (because $f - c X_{n+1}^m \notin R_0[X_1,X_{n+1}]$),
$B$ has transcendence degree at least $2$ over $B_0$; so the prime ideal $B_+ = \bigoplus_{i>0} B_i$ has height at least $2$.
We showed:
$$
\text{$B$ is an $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$-graded normal affine ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-domain such that $	\operatorname{\text{\rm ht}}(B_+)\ge2$.}
$$
Since $B/x_{n+1}B \cong R/fR$ is a domain, $x_{n+1}$ is a homogeneous prime element of $B$ of degree $1$.
We claim that 
\begin{equation}  \label {K5f43d32rcnA391Hi02r5}
B_{(x_{n+1})} \cong R/(f - c) .
\end{equation}
To see this, let $\varphi : R \to B_{(x_{n+1})}$ be the surjective ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-homomorphism defined by $\varphi( X_i ) = x_i / x_{n+1}^{d_i}$ ($1 \le i \le n$).
We have $\varphi(f) = f\big( {x_1}/{x_{n+1}^{d_1}} , \dots, {x_n}/{x_{n+1}^{d_n}} \big) = f / x_{n+1}^m = c$,
so $(f-c) \subseteq \ker\varphi$.
Lemma \ref{9823bSnby5is5wckdsohf} implies that $f-c$ is a prime element of $R$, so $(f-c)$ is a height $1$ prime ideal of $R$.
Since $\dim R = n$ and $\dim B_{(x_{n+1})} = \dim 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Proj}} B = n-1$, $\ker\varphi$ is a height $1$ prime ideal of $R$, so $\ker\varphi = (f-c)$,
which proves \eqref{K5f43d32rcnA391Hi02r5}.

Since $B$ is an $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$-graded domain and $x_{n+1}$ is a homogeneous prime element of $B$ of positive degree, we have $\big( B_{(x_{n+1})} \big)^* = B_0^*$.
Since $\deg(f - cX_{n+1}^m)>0$, $B_0 = {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}[X_1, \dots, X_{n+1}]_0 = {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}^{[{r}]}$ for some $r\ge0$, so $\big( B_{(x_{n+1})} \big)^* = B_0^* = {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}^*$.
It then follows from \eqref{K5f43d32rcnA391Hi02r5} that $R/(f-c)$ has trivial units.

Suppose that $R/fR$ is rigid and 
let us apply Thm \ref{7654cvhgfsd2d34fds23f42dfdghjk8l} to $B$ and $x = x_{n+1}$ (note that $d = \deg(x) = 1$).
By that result and the fact that $(B/xB)^{(d)} = B/xB = B/x_{n+1}B \cong R/fR$ is rigid, we obtain that $B_{(x_{n+1})}$ is rigid,
so $R/(f-c)$ is rigid by \eqref{K5f43d32rcnA391Hi02r5}.

label: 24799F47-1201-4FF5-A50D-93EB60154D1C
title: Remark
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Let $n \ge 2$ and define
$$
B_n = \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}[X_0, \dots, X_n] / (X_0^3 + \cdots + X_n^3 )
\quad \text{and} \quad
A_n = \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}[X_0, \dots, X_n] / (X_0^3 + \cdots + X_n^3 - 1) .
$$
\begin{enumerata}

\item $A_n$ and $B_n$ are domains with trivial units, and of Krull dimension $n$.

\item $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}} A_n$ is a smooth affine variety, and if $n$ is even then $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}} A_n$ is rational.

\item $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}} B_n$ is a normal affine variety, and if $n$ is odd then $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}} B_n$ is rational.



\item If $n \in \{2,3,4\}$ then  $B_n^{(d)}$ is rigid for all $d\ge1$ and $A_n$ is rigid.

\end{enumerata}
To prove these claims, consider
$f_n = X_0^3 + \cdots + X_n^3 \in R_n = \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}[X_0, \dots, X_n] = \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}^{[n+1]}$ where $X_0,\dots,X_{n}$ are homogeneous of degree $1$.
We have $B_n = R_n/(f_n)$ and $A_n = R_n/(f_n-1)$, so Proposition \ref{u65vmklio909543qsdfh4vue} implies (in particular)
that $A_n$ and $B_n$ are domains with trivial units. So (a) is true.
It is clear that $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}} A_n$ is smooth and that $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}} B_n$ is normal.
Note that the open subset ``$X_{n+1} \neq 0$'' of the Fermat cubic $\EuScript{F}_n = \ensuremath{\mathbb{V}}_{\!+}(X_0^3 + \cdots + X_n^3 + X_{n+1}^3) \subset \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^{n+1}$
is isomorphic to $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}} A_n$;
if $n$ is even then $\EuScript{F}_n$ is rational by Rem.\ \ref{24799F47-1201-4FF5-A50D-93EB60154D1C}, so $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}} A_n$ is rational. This proves (b).
Since $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Proj}} B_n = \EuScript{F}_{n-1}$, we have the birational equivalences
$	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}} B_n \sim \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^1 \times 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Proj}} B_n \sim \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^1 \times \EuScript{F}_{n-1}$;
if $n$ is odd then $\EuScript{F}_{n-1}$ is rational by Rem.\ \ref{24799F47-1201-4FF5-A50D-93EB60154D1C}, so $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}} B_n$ is rational. This proves (c).

It is easy to see that $B_n$ is saturated in codimension $1$ (for instance this follows from Lemma \ref{o8y7t626rf53deg23489jru3sgbref6}).
So Cor.\ \ref{1D0x2mv4yhhtfukCs1unc3t46bisgf9f2} implies that, for each $n\ge2$,
the rings $B_n^{(d)}$ ($d \ge 1$) all have the same rigidity status.
Combining that with part (b) of Prop.\ \ref{u65vmklio909543qsdfh4vue} gives:
$$
\text{if $n$ is such that $B_n$ is rigid, then  $B_n^{(d)}$ is rigid for all $d\ge1$ and $A_n$ is rigid.}
$$
So, in order to prove (d), it suffices to show that $B_2$, $B_3$ and $B_4$ are rigid.
Since $\mathscr{P}(3)$ and $\mathscr{P}(4)$ are true (see \ref{ConjPn}), the rings $B_2 \cong B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}; 3,3,3}$ and $B_3 \cong B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}; 3,3,3,3}$ are rigid.
Since $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Proj}} B_4 = \EuScript{F}_3$ does not contain a cylinder by \ref{24799F47-1201-4FF5-A50D-93EB60154D1C},
it follows that $B_4$ is rigid by Thm \ref{edh83yf6r79hvujhxu6wrefji9e}.
This proves (d).
(More generally, if $\mathscr{P}(n+1)$ is true or $\EuScript{F}_{n-1}$ does not contain a cylinder then $B_n$ is rigid.)


                                                                      
                                                         
                                                                                                                                           

Note that the rigidity of $A_3$ can be proved without invoking Proposition~\ref{u65vmklio909543qsdfh4vue}:
since $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}} A_3$ is an open subset of $\EuScript{F}_3$,
\ref{24799F47-1201-4FF5-A50D-93EB60154D1C} implies that $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}} A_3$ does not contain a cylinder, so $A_3$ is rigid by \ref{jbhgfdxfewae33w6q920we}.
In contrast, the proofs of rigidity for $A_2$ and $A_4$ appear to require the Proposition.
Moreover, the rigidity of $A_2$ and $A_4$ is noteworthy, since $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}} A_2$ and $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}} A_4$ are smooth, rational, and have trivial units.

label: 1hfcvbnn92m3n456789df7nm534jh5f6d78
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label {1hfcvbnn92m3n456789df7nm534jh5f6d78}
Let $H$ be a subgroup of a finitely generated abelian group $G$ such that $G/H$ is not torsion.
Let $\EuScript{H}(H,G)$ be the set of all subgroups $H'$ of $G$ such that $H \subseteq H' \subset G$ and $G/H' \cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$.
Then $\EuScript{H}(H,G) \neq \varnothing$ and the intersection of all elements of $\EuScript{H}(H,G)$ is $	\operatorname{\text{\rm torc}}(H,G)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Viewing $G$ as a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-module, let $S = \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \setminus \{0\}$ and consider the $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}$-vector space $G_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}} = S^{-1}G$
and the canonical homomorphism $\lambda : G \to G_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}$, $x \mapsto x/1$.
For each subgroup $K$ of $G$, let $K_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}$ be the subspace $S^{-1}K$ of $G_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}$ and note that $\lambda^{-1}( K_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}} ) = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm torc}}(K,G)$.

Since  $G/H$ is not torsion, there exists $y \in G \setminus 	\operatorname{\text{\rm torc}}(H,G)$.
Consider any such $y$.  Consider the vector $\lambda(y) \in G_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}$ and note that $\lambda(y) \notin H_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}$.
Choose a vector subspace $V_y$ of $G_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}$ such that $H_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}} \subseteq V_y \subset G_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}$, $\dim_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}(G_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}} / V_y) = 1$, and $\lambda(y) \notin V_y$.
Let $H_y = \lambda^{-1}(V_y)$. Then $y \notin H_y$ and $H \subseteq H_y \subset G$; since $G/H_y$ is torsion-free (and hence free, since $G$ is finitely generated),
and since $S^{-1}( G/H_y ) \cong G_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}} / V_y \cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}$, we have $G/H_y \cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$; so $H_y \in \EuScript{H}(H,G)$. 
This shows that $\EuScript{H}(H,G) \neq \varnothing$ and $y \notin I$, where $I$ denotes the intersection of all elements of $\EuScript{H}(H,G)$.
This being true for each $y \in G \setminus 	\operatorname{\text{\rm torc}}(H,G)$, we obtain $I \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm torc}}(H,G)$, and the reverse inclusion is clear.

body_md:
\label {8A76f5swaz23edafgwuvperol0ut83m395ff}
Let $B = \bigoplus_{i \in G} B_i$ be a domain graded by an abelian group $G$ and let $H$ be a subgroup of $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)$.
Let $\Omega = \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)/H$ and let $\pi : \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) \to \Omega$ be the canonical homomorphism of the quotient group.
Let $\EuScript{B}$ denote the ring $B$  endowed with the $\Omega$-grading defined by
$\EuScript{B} = \bigoplus_{\omega \in \Omega} \EuScript{B}_\omega$, where $\EuScript{B}_\omega = \bigoplus_{ \pi(i)=\omega } B_i$ for each $\omega \in \Omega$.
We refer to this as ``the natural $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)/H$-grading''.
It satisfies $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}( \EuScript{B} ) = \Omega$. Observe that $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1( \EuScript{B} ) = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B)$ and let us show that
\begin{equation} \label {765O043wsdvbnm32M91q0oijhbLvcl}
\pi\big( \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} ) \big) =  \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( \EuScript{B} , {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} ) \quad \text{for every ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B)$.}
\end{equation}
Indeed, let  ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B)$. If $i \in {\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} )$ then $B_i \nsubseteq {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$,
so $\EuScript{B}_{ \pi(i) }  \nsubseteq {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ (because $B_i \subseteq \EuScript{B}_{ \pi(i) }$) and hence $\pi(i) \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}( \EuScript{B}, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} )$.
Thus, $\pi \big(  {\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} ) \big) \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}( \EuScript{B}, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} )$.
Conversely, consider $\omega \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}( \EuScript{B}, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} )$. Then $\EuScript{B}_\omega  = \bigoplus_{ \pi(i)=\omega } B_i$ is not included in ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$,
so there exists $i \in \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)$ such that $\pi(i)=\omega$ and $B_i \nsubseteq {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$; then $i \in {\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} )$ and hence
$\omega \in \pi \big(  {\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} ) \big)$.
This shows that $\pi \big( {\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} ) \big) = \ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}( \EuScript{B}, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} )$, and it follows that
$\pi \big(  \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} ) \big) = \overline\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}( \EuScript{B}, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} )$.
So \eqref{765O043wsdvbnm32M91q0oijhbLvcl} is proved.
({\it Caution:} Assertion \eqref{765O043wsdvbnm32M91q0oijhbLvcl} implies that $\pi\big( \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) \big) \subseteq \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(\EuScript{B})$,
but equality does not necessarily hold.)

label: p0987uhmnbvccjiuseyt428
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label {p0987uhmnbvccjiuseyt428}
\it Let ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and $B$ a normal affine ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-domain graded over ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ by an abelian group $G$.
Assume that $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)/\operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)$ is not torsion and define $r = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm rank}}\big( \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) / \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) \big)$ and $W = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm torc}}(\operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B),\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B))$.
\begin{enumerata}

\item There exists ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B)$ such that $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)/\overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} )$ is not torsion.
Consider such a ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ and define
$\EuScript{H}_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} = \EuScript{H}\big( \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} ) , \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) \big)$ and $T_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm torc}}( \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} ) , \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) )$.
Then the following hold.
\begin{enumerata}

\item $\EuScript{H}_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \neq \varnothing$

\item For each $H \in \EuScript{H}_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$, there exists $D \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm LND}}(B)$ such that $\ker(D) = B^{(H)}$.

\item There exists a subset $\Delta_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ of $	\operatorname{\text{\rm LND}}(B)$ such that $\bigcap_{D \in \Delta_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}} \ker(D) = B^{ ( T_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} ) }$.

\end{enumerata}

\item There exists a subset $\Delta$ of $	\operatorname{\text{\rm LND}}(B)$ such that $\bigcap_{D \in \Delta} \ker(D) = B^{ (W) }$.

\item There exists a field $K$ such that
$$
\text{$	\operatorname{\text{\rm ML}}(B) \subseteq B^{(W)} \subseteq K \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Frac}}(B)$ \ \ and \ \ $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Frac}}(B) = K^{(r)}$.}
$$
In particular, $	\operatorname{\text{\rm trdeg}}( B : 	\operatorname{\text{\rm ML}}(B) ) \ge r$.

\item $B$ is non-rigid, and if $G$ is torsion-free then $\mathscr{X}(B) = \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}(B)$.

\end{enumerata}

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $B$ is ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-affine and the grading is over ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$, $B$ is finitely generated as a $B_0$-algebra and $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)$ is finitely generated.
Consequently, $r$ is finite (so $r \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} \setminus \{0\}$).

(a) If $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B) = \varnothing$ then $\operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) = \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)$ by definition, contradicting the assumption that $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)/\operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)$ is not torsion.
So $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B) \neq \varnothing$.

By Prop.\  \ref{89fDCN584uKHJu7u59034uf}, the nonempty set $\big\{\, \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} ) \, \mid \, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B) \, \big\}$ is finite.
So we can choose ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_1, \dots, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_n \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B)$ such that $\operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) =  \bigcap_{i=1}^n\overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_i )$.
There must exist $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ such that $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)/\overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_i )$ is not torsion.
This proves the first claim in assertion (a).

Consider ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B)$ such that $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)/\overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} )$ is not torsion and define
$\EuScript{H}_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ and $T_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ as in the statement of (a).
Lemma \ref{1hfcvbnn92m3n456789df7nm534jh5f6d78} implies that $\EuScript{H}_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \neq \varnothing$ (which proves (a-i)) and
\begin{equation}  \label {1Adcdb9bdNTs438ywte6v2w89unvBNZjxmnbevCe49831}
\textstyle \bigcap_{ H \in \EuScript{H}_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} } H  = T_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} .
\end{equation}
Let $H \in \EuScript{H}_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$. Let $\pi : \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) \to \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)/H$ be the canonical homomorphism.
The definition of $\EuScript{H}_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ implies that $\overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} ) \subseteq H = \ker(\pi)$ and $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)/H \cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$.
Let $\EuScript{B}(H)$ denote the ring $B$ endowed with the natural $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)/H$-grading (see paragraph \ref{8A76f5swaz23edafgwuvperol0ut83m395ff})
and note that $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}( \EuScript{B}(H) ) = \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)/H \cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$.
Since $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B) = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1( \EuScript{B}(H) )$, we have ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1( \EuScript{B}(H) )$; thus,
$$
\textstyle
\operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}( \EuScript{B}(H) ) \ = \ \bigcap_{ {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{q}}} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1( \EuScript{B}(H) ) } \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( \EuScript{B}(H), {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{q}}} ) \ \subseteq \  
\overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( \EuScript{B}(H), {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} )  = \pi\big( \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} ) \big) = 0 
$$
where the penultimate equality follows from \eqref{765O043wsdvbnm32M91q0oijhbLvcl}.
Since $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}( \EuScript{B}(H) ) \cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$ and $\operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}( \EuScript{B}(H) ) = 0$,
Cor.\ \ref{i8976r53g47c8ru3yd3g23ev5627fu} implies that there exists $D \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm HLND}}( \EuScript{B}(H) )$ such that $\ker( D ) = \EuScript{B}(H)_0 = B^{(H)}$.
Since $D \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm LND}}(B)$, this proves (a-ii).
Since $H$ is a proper subgroup of $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)$, we have $B^{(H)} \neq B$ and hence $D \neq 0$. So $B$ is non-rigid (this is claimed in (d)).

For each $H \in \EuScript{H}_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$, choose $D_H \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm LND}}(B)$ such that $\ker(D_H) = B^{(H)}$ (possible by (a-ii)).
Define $\Delta_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} = \big\{\, D_H \, \mid \, H \in \EuScript{H}_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \, \big\}$.
Then $\bigcap_{D \in \Delta_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}} \ker(D) = \bigcap_{H \in \EuScript{H}_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}} B^{(H)} = B^{ ( T_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} ) }$,
the last equality by \eqref{1Adcdb9bdNTs438ywte6v2w89unvBNZjxmnbevCe49831}.
This proves (a-iii) and completes the proof of (a).

(b) Recall that we chose ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_1, \dots, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_n \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B)$ such that $\operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) =  \bigcap_{i=1}^n\overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_i )$,
and that we noted that $I \neq \varnothing$, where 
$$
I = \big\{\, i \, \mid \, \text{$1 \le i \le n$ and $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) /  \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_i )$ is not torsion} \, \big\} .
$$
Since $\operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) =  \bigcap_{i=1}^n\overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_i )$,
Lemma \ref{jhgf09wk2mnddm9ijh2wedfgj34b} gives $W = \bigcap_{i=1}^n 	\operatorname{\text{\rm torc}}\big( \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_i ) , \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) \big)$.
We have
$	\operatorname{\text{\rm torc}}\big( \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_i ) , \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) \big) = T_{{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_i}$ for each $i \in I$
and $	\operatorname{\text{\rm torc}}\big( \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_i ) , \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) \big) = \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)$ for each $i \in \{1,\dots,n\} \setminus I$, so 
\begin{equation} \label {u6f5c263F7v8b92ne8fbvcx23iawekeo09}
\textstyle W = \bigcap_{i = 1}^n 	\operatorname{\text{\rm torc}}\big( \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}( B, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_i ) , \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) \big) = \bigcap_{i \in I} T_{{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_i} .
\end{equation}
For each $i \in I$, consider a subset $\Delta_{{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_i}$ of $	\operatorname{\text{\rm LND}}(B)$ such that $\bigcap_{D \in \Delta_{{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_i}} \ker(D) = B^{ ( T_{{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_i} ) }$
($\Delta_{{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_i}$ exists by (a-iii)).
Let $\Delta = \bigcup_{i \in I} \Delta_{{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_i}$. Then
$$
\textstyle
\bigcap_{D \in \Delta} \ker(D)
= \bigcap_{i \in I} \bigcap_{D \in \Delta_{{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_i}} \ker(D)
= \bigcap_{i \in I} B^{ ( T_{{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_i} ) }
= B^{ (W) } 
$$
where the last equality follows from \eqref{u6f5c263F7v8b92ne8fbvcx23iawekeo09}. This proves (b).


(c) Let $R$ denote $B$ endowed with the natural $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)/W$-grading (see paragraph \ref{8A76f5swaz23edafgwuvperol0ut83m395ff}).
Since  $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(R) = \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)/W$ is finitely generated and torsion-free,
and $	\operatorname{\text{\rm rank}}( \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)/W ) = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm rank}}( \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)/\operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) ) = r \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} \setminus \{0\}$, we have $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(R) \cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^r$.
Lemma \ref{i8765redfvbnki8765rfghytrew123456789iuhv}
implies that there exists a field $K$ such that $R_0 \subseteq K \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Frac}}(R)$ and $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Frac}}(R) = K^{(r)}$.
Since $R_0 = B^{(W)} \supseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm ML}}(B)$ by (b), we have $	\operatorname{\text{\rm ML}}(B) \subseteq K$. Since $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Frac}}(B)=	\operatorname{\text{\rm Frac}}(R)$, (c) follows.

(d) We already proved that $B$ is non-rigid.
If moreover $G$ is torsion-free then Lemma \ref{876543wsdfgxhnm290cAo} implies that $	\operatorname{\text{\rm HLND}}(B) \neq \{0\}$,
so Thm \ref{8237e9d1983hdjyev93}(c)  gives $\mathscr{X}(B) = \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}(B)$.
